name: Game Development
description: Game loops, delta time, ECS, physics, Unity/Unreal/Godot fundamentals and performance discipline.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Game Development is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is a game engine?
cards.answer: A framework that provides the common machinery games need — rendering, physics, audio, input, animation, asset management and an editor — so developers focus on the game itself. Unity, Unreal Engine and Godot are the best known.
cards.explanation: Writing an engine from scratch teaches a lot but takes years; most commercial games use an existing engine and customise it.

cards.prompt: Which languages are used to make games?
cards.answer: C++ for engines and performance-critical games (Unreal Engine), C# for Unity games, GDScript or C# in Godot, plus Lua and other scripting languages embedded for gameplay logic. JavaScript/TypeScript targets browser games.
cards.explanation: Engines often split the work: a fast core in C++ and gameplay written in an easier scripting language that designers can change quickly.

cards.prompt: What is the game loop?
cards.answer: The endless loop at the heart of every game: read input, update the game state (movement, physics, AI), render the frame, repeat — typically 30 to 144+ times per second.
cards.explanation: Each pass is one frame. Everything in a game must fit within the frame budget — about 16.7 ms at 60 frames per second — or the game stutters.

cards.prompt: What do frame rate (FPS) and frame time mean?
cards.answer: Frame rate is how many frames are drawn per second; frame time is how long each one takes. 60 FPS means a budget of 16.7 ms per frame; 120 FPS means 8.3 ms.
cards.explanation: Consistent frame times matter more than a high average: a game averaging 60 FPS with occasional 50 ms spikes feels worse than a steady 45 FPS.

cards.prompt: What are sprites and meshes?
cards.answer: A sprite is a 2D image drawn on screen (a character, an item) — the building block of 2D games. A mesh is a 3D shape made of triangles (vertices and faces), covered with textures — the building block of 3D games.
cards.explanation: GPUs are built to draw enormous numbers of textured triangles quickly, which is why even 2D engines often draw sprites as two triangles forming a rectangle.

modules.name: Engine Fundamentals
modules.description: The loop, time, and the architecture patterns games are built on.

cards.prompt: What does a game loop do, and why is physics usually on a fixed timestep?
cards.answer: Each frame: process input, update simulation, render. Physics runs on a fixed timestep accumulator so the simulation is deterministic and stable regardless of frame rate, with rendering interpolating between physics states.
cards.explanation: Variable-timestep physics behaves differently at 30 and 144 fps — collisions tunnel and integrators blow up. The standard structure accumulates real time and runs zero or more fixed steps per frame, which is Unity's FixedUpdate and Unreal's substepping.

resources.title: Gaffer On Games — Fix your timestep

cards.prompt: Why does this player move faster on a 144 Hz monitor?
cards.answer: The movement is per frame, not per second. Multiply by `Time.deltaTime` so speed is expressed in units per second and is frame-rate independent.
cards.explanation: Every per-frame change — movement, rotation, timers, lerps — needs delta time. The classic follow-up bug is `Lerp(a, b, deltaTime)`, which is frame-rate dependent smoothing; use `1 - exp(-k * dt)` when you need a stable exponential ease.

cards.prompt: Object-oriented game objects vs entity-component-system
cards.answer: OO puts data and behaviour in deep inheritance hierarchies; ECS separates entities (ids), components (plain data) and systems (behaviour over component queries).

left.title: GameObject / inheritance
points: Intuitive: a Player is a Character is an Entity

cards.explanation: ECS exists because of the memory wall: iterating 10,000 positions packed in an array is far faster than chasing 10,000 scattered objects. Unity DOTS, Bevy and most modern engines lean this way for simulation-heavy code.

cards.prompt: Unity vs Unreal vs Godot
cards.answer: Unity: C#, huge asset ecosystem, strongest for mobile and mid-scale 3D/2D. Unreal: C++ and Blueprints, best-in-class rendering, AAA and cinematics. Godot: GDScript/C#, tiny, free and open source, excellent 2D.

left.title: Unity / Unreal
points: Unity: fastest iteration, biggest job market
Unity: royalty-free tiers, licence history is a real risk factor
Unreal: 5% royalty past a revenue threshold

right.title: Godot
points: MIT licensed — no fees, no rug pulls

cards.explanation: Pick by project shape and team skills, not by engine loyalty. Prototype in whichever you can iterate fastest with — the engine matters far less to a finished game than scope control does.

modules.name: Systems & Performance
modules.description: Collision, state machines, memory discipline and shipping something playable.

cards.prompt: How does collision detection avoid checking every pair of objects?
cards.answer: In two phases. Broad phase uses a spatial structure (uniform grid, quadtree/octree, BVH, sweep and prune) to find candidate pairs cheaply. Narrow phase does exact tests (SAT, GJK) only on those candidates.
cards.explanation: Naive all-pairs is O(n²) — 1,000 objects is 500,000 tests per frame. Broad phase cuts that to near-linear. The other classic issue is tunnelling: a fast object skipping through a thin wall, solved with continuous collision detection or swept tests.

cards.prompt: Your player controller is a thicket of booleans: isJumping, isAttacking, isDashing. What is the fix?
cards.answer: A finite state machine: one explicit state at a time with defined transitions. Each state owns its enter, update and exit behaviour, and impossible combinations become unrepresentable.
cards.explanation: N booleans give 2^N combinations, most of them invalid — that is where 'attacking while dashing while dead' bugs come from. Hierarchical state machines handle shared behaviour (all airborne states), and behaviour trees scale better for complex AI.

cards.prompt: Your bullet-hell game stutters every few seconds. What is the likely cause?
cards.answer: Garbage collection pauses from allocating and destroying hundreds of objects per second. Pool them: pre-allocate a fixed set, deactivate instead of destroying, and reuse.
cards.explanation: In a 60 fps game the entire frame budget is 16.6 ms, so even a 10 ms GC pause is a visible hitch. Pooling also avoids fragmentation and instantiation cost. Watch for per-frame allocations hiding in string concatenation, LINQ and boxing.

cards.prompt: What is the per-frame time budget at 60 fps and at 144 fps?
cards.answer: 16.7 ms at 60 fps, 6.9 ms at 144 fps — for everything: input, simulation, physics, rendering and presentation.
cards.explanation: That budget is the discipline of game programming. Profile before optimising — the culprit is usually draw calls, an unbatched material, an O(n²) loop over entities, or GC. Frame *consistency* matters more than average fps: a steady 60 beats a spiky 90.

cards.prompt: Why do most hobby games never ship, and what actually helps?
cards.answer: Scope. The fix is brutal reduction: build the core loop first, make it fun with placeholder art, and cut everything that does not serve it. Ship something small and finished before something large and imagined.
cards.explanation: Vertical slice over horizontal features: one complete level beats twelve half-systems. Playtest early with someone who has never seen it — you cannot feel your own game's onboarding. And engine work is not progress unless it is on the critical path.

modules.name: Core Game Systems
modules.description: Input, cameras, scene graphs, physics engines, animation, audio, save systems and asset pipelines.

cards.prompt: How should a game handle input so it is responsive and rebindable?
cards.answer: Map raw device events to abstract actions ("jump", "move") through a binding layer, so controls can be rebound and multiple devices supported. Poll or collect input once per frame, buffer short presses so a quick tap between frames is not lost, and apply dead zones to analogue sticks.
cards.explanation: Input buffering and "coyote time" (allowing a jump a few frames after leaving a ledge) make controls feel fair rather than strictly accurate. Engines provide action-mapping systems — Unity's Input System, Unreal's Enhanced Input, Godot's InputMap.

cards.prompt: What makes a third-person or platformer camera feel good?
cards.answer: Smooth follow with damping rather than rigid attachment, look-ahead in the direction of movement, dead zones so small movements do not jiggle the view, collision handling so walls do not block the view, and framing that shows what the player needs to see next.
cards.explanation: Use frame-rate-independent smoothing (exponential decay with delta time) or the camera will behave differently at different frame rates. Screen shake and zoom should be subtle and optional — they cause motion sickness for some players.

cards.prompt: What is a scene graph, and how do parent–child transforms work?
cards.answer: A tree of objects where each node's transform (position, rotation, scale) is relative to its parent. A node's world transform is its parent's world transform multiplied by its own local one, so moving a ship moves everything attached to it.
cards.explanation: Hierarchies simplify attaching weapons to hands or wheels to cars, but deep hierarchies cost CPU to update every frame, and non-uniform scaling on parents can skew children. Engines cache world transforms and recompute only when something changes (a dirty flag).

cards.prompt: What does a rigid-body physics engine do each step?
cards.answer: Integrates forces into velocities and positions, detects collisions (broad then narrow phase), and resolves them by solving contact and joint constraints — applying impulses so objects bounce, slide and stack plausibly — at a fixed timestep.
cards.explanation: Physics engines trade accuracy for speed and stability. Moving objects by setting positions directly bypasses the solver and causes tunnelling and jitter — move physics objects through forces or velocities. Keep mass ratios reasonable; very light objects on very heavy ones destabilise stacks.

cards.prompt: How do skeletal animation, blending and animation state machines work together?
cards.answer: A mesh is skinned to a skeleton of bones; animation clips store bone transforms over time. Blending interpolates between clips (walk into run by speed, via blend trees) and transitions crossfade between states in an animation state machine driven by gameplay parameters.
cards.explanation: Root motion lets the animation drive the character's movement, trading control for realism. Inverse kinematics adjusts limbs at runtime (feet on uneven ground, hands on ledges). Keep gameplay logic authoritative and let animation follow it, or controls feel sluggish.

cards.prompt: How should a game save and load player progress safely?
cards.answer: Serialise a versioned data model of the game state (not engine objects) to a stable format; write to a temporary file and atomically rename it over the old save; keep a backup slot; and migrate old versions forward when loading. Saved references use stable IDs rather than memory pointers.
cards.explanation: Players lose saves to crashes during writing and to updates that change the format — both are preventable. Validate loaded data, since saves can be edited, and treat save-file parsing like any untrusted input in multiplayer or shared contexts.

cards.prompt: What does an asset pipeline do?
cards.answer: It converts source assets — models, textures, audio, levels — from authoring formats into optimised runtime formats per platform: compressed textures with mipmaps, optimised meshes and LODs, compressed audio, packed bundles. It tracks dependencies so only changed assets rebuild.
cards.explanation: Import settings are as important as code: a 4K texture on a small prop, or uncompressed audio, silently blows memory budgets. Large binary assets need Git LFS or a dedicated version-control system (Perforce is common in games).

modules.name: Multiplayer, AI & Generation
modules.description: Networked game architectures, lag compensation and rollback, behaviour trees and utility AI, procedural generation and determinism.

cards.prompt: Authoritative server vs peer-to-peer lockstep
cards.answer: With an authoritative server, clients send inputs and the server simulates the true game state, sending results back — cheat-resistant and scalable to many players. Peer-to-peer lockstep has every peer simulate the same deterministic game from shared inputs — little bandwidth, but it needs perfect determinism and waits for the slowest peer.

right.title: P2P lockstep
points: Every peer runs the same simulation
Desyncs and waiting on slow peers

cards.explanation: Competitive action games use authoritative servers with client-side prediction and interpolation to hide latency; strategy games with thousands of units traditionally use lockstep. Never trust the client for anything that matters — that is where cheats live.

cards.prompt: What are client-side prediction, server reconciliation and rollback netcode?
cards.answer: Prediction applies the player's own input immediately instead of waiting for the server; reconciliation corrects the local state when the authoritative update arrives, replaying unacknowledged inputs. Rollback (fighting games) predicts the opponent's input, and when the real input differs, rewinds to that frame and re-simulates forward.
cards.explanation: All three hide latency by guessing and correcting. Rollback requires cheap save/restore of full game state and deterministic simulation. Server-side lag compensation rewinds hitboxes to what the shooter saw, which is why you sometimes get hit after reaching cover.

resources.title: Gabriel Gambetta — Client-side prediction and server reconciliation

cards.prompt: Finite state machines vs behaviour trees vs utility AI for game characters
cards.answer: FSMs switch between explicit states with transitions; behaviour trees compose reusable tasks with selectors (try alternatives) and sequences (do in order), re-evaluated each tick; utility AI scores every possible action by weighted considerations and picks the best.

left.title: FSM / behaviour tree
points: FSM: simple, becomes spaghetti at scale

cards.explanation: FSMs get tangled as states multiply; behaviour trees scale to complex, modular behaviours and are standard in engines; utility AI produces more emergent, context-sensitive choices at the cost of tuning curves. Many games mix them — a tree whose leaves use utility scoring.

cards.prompt: How is procedural content generated, and why use noise rather than plain randomness?
cards.answer: Algorithms create content from rules and randomness: terrain from layered gradient noise (Perlin, simplex) at several frequencies (octaves), dungeons from room placement plus corridors or cellular automata, and variety from seeded random number generators.
cards.explanation: Pure randomness looks like static; coherent noise varies smoothly, producing natural hills and coastlines. Seeding makes worlds reproducible — same seed, same world — which enables sharing, debugging and generating on demand instead of storing everything.

resources.title: Red Blob Games — Making maps with noise functions

cards.prompt: Your lockstep multiplayer game desyncs between a Windows PC and a Mac after a few minutes. What are the usual causes?
cards.answer: Non-determinism: floating-point results that differ across compilers, CPU instruction sets or maths libraries; iteration over unordered hash maps; random number generators seeded or called differently; time-based logic using the wall clock; and frame-rate-dependent updates.
cards.explanation: Deterministic simulations use fixed timesteps, seeded RNGs advanced identically, ordered containers, and often fixed-point maths for the simulation. Hash the game state each tick and compare across peers to detect the exact frame a desync began.

resources.title: Gaffer On Games — Floating point determinism
